It is tolerable because the structural chunker is an opt-in experimental mode that already fails open for every expected condition by design, the substituted output is the exact default-mode chunker for that file (complete and correct, only differently split), and nothing can be returned empty or wrong. The cost is retrieval-quality only, plus a silent defect in the structural path going unnoticed; there is no disclosure channel for it.

evidence: except Exception around the tree-sitter parse, text re-read, leaf-unit extraction, merge and chunk materialisation falls back to _chunk_file_line_windows(file_path) with no record of the cause. Accepted because the mode is opt-in, the fallback produces complete correct line-window chunks, and the index records the chunker mode as a whole, so quality degrades but correctness holds. evidence: except Exception around model.encode(texts) and np.asarray(raw, dtype=float32); any raw RuntimeError or numpy ValueError (ragged nested sequence) is re-raised as BackendExecutionError('dense model encode failed for N input(s)') from the original. It never returns an empty or partial matrix, so the semantic leg cannot silently vanish from a ranking.

The pinned-checksum gate that follows means a failed download can never be installed as if it were the model. Safe direction: raise, no install.

evidence: except Exception wraps the whole psutil path (import psutil, Process(pid), enumerate children, terminate, wait_procs, kill survivors) and falls through with pass to the OS-native killer (taskkill /T /F on Windows, killpg/os.kill elsewhere). An ImportError for the optional psutil, NoSuchProcess for an already-exited child, or any mid-sequence psutil fault all take that route. On the Windows fallback the return value is [pid] whether or not taskkill succeeded, because check=False discards its exit status.
reason: Best-effort cleanup of a timed-out readiness child where psutil is an optional dependency: falling back to the platform killer is the intended redundancy, and the caller's verdict (returncode forced to 1, timeout report) does not depend on the kill succeeding. Caveat recorded: killed_process_ids can over-report on the Windows fallback; it is a diagnostic field, not a safety signal, so this is not treated as a fail-open.

evidence: except Exception around the POSIX killpg(pid, SIGTERM), sleep, killpg(pid, SIGKILL) sequence (also reached when os.killpg is absent via the deliberate AttributeError); any failure, such as ProcessLookupError because the group already exited or PermissionError, falls through to a per-pid os.kill(pid, SIGKILL) attempt.
reason: Escalation ladder for stopping a runaway child: group kill first, single-process kill second. Both steps are idempotent, a group that is already gone is the success case rather than an error, and the next rung is guarded by its own handler. Nothing downstream consumes a result that this fallthrough could corrupt.

evidence: Inner except Exception around os.kill(pid, SIGKILL) is pass: when the last-resort kill fails (ProcessLookupError for an already-dead pid, PermissionError for a foreign one) the function returns whatever pids were recorded so far, possibly an empty list. The caller stores that list as killed_process_ids in the timeout report with no flag distinguishing 'nothing to kill' from 'could not kill'.
reason: Discarded on purpose because the process usually has already exited and the timeout verdict is failed regardless, so no result is made to look better. It is still a swallow: a surviving orphan child would be indistinguishable from a clean exit apart from an empty killed_process_ids list. Accepted for a diagnostic-only field in a dogfood harness; a future hardening could record a kill_failed marker.

evidence: After a subprocess.TimeoutExpired and tree termination, except Exception around process.communicate(timeout=POST_TIMEOUT_COMMUNICATE_SECONDS) is pass: if draining the dead child's pipes fails or times out, stdout and stderr keep the partial text captured from the TimeoutExpired exception (possibly empty) and the timeout report is built from them. The report still sets returncode = 1 and a failed timeout result.
reason: The verdict is already failed and fixed before this handler runs, so the swallow can only lose diagnostic tail lines, never turn a failure into a pass. It stays a silent swallow because the report does not say the post-kill drain failed, so empty stdout_tail and stderr_tail look like 'child produced no output'. Safe direction for the verdict; diagnostics are best-effort.

evidence: except Exception around the ledger_store.resolve_agent_id and list_claims probe for foreign claims: on any failure _foreign is set to an empty list, so the foreign_claims and foreign_claim_count keys are simply not emitted. It is tolerated only because the claim hook is advisory coordination, not a gate, and failing prepare's primary read over it would be worse; the cost is a missed coordination warning, not a wrong edit target.

Not failing the whole prepare read is the documented advisory contract (submit_claim itself never blocks), which makes this a visible degrade, not a swallow.

evidence: except Exception around the atomic swap of the staged Node runtime into place and the check that the node executable exists: it removes the half-installed runtime directory, restores the backed-up previous runtime when one existed, and then re-raises with a bare raise. The caller still sees the original exception.

It catches Exception rather than BaseException on purpose; interrupts are not rolled back here, which is a separate matter from this record.

It degrades rather than raises so the other languages and the toolchain installers can still be attempted in the same run.

The error is reported, not hidden, so this is a logged degrade with the failure visible in the structured result.

evidence: except Exception around wrapper_backend.search_project(root, config_path): the exception is discarded without a log, a note or a flag, and every rule in wrapper_rules is appended to other_resolved bound to the same wrapper backend, so it is re-run one rule at a time through the per-rule search path. It is tolerated because the fallback runs the same backend and its own failures still propagate, so a rule is not silently skipped; this is a swallow of the cause, not of the outcome.

The exception text is kept in the failure line and the broad catch lets the remaining cases still run and be reported.

This is a deliberate two-step version fallback for source checkouts and editable installs where the distribution is not registered, so the first swallow is expected to fire there. It is still a swallow because a degraded value is printed without disclosure; the consequence is a wrong version string, not wrong search behaviour or a misrouted command.

It is a degrade rather than a boundary because the call still succeeds with a different engine, and the cause is kept rather than dropped. evidence: except Exception around the DirectoryScanner walk and the per-file, per-pattern backend.search loop (the earlier ImportError clause is a separate narrow handler): it returns an empty stdout, stderr built by _gpu_runtime_error as 'GPU search failed for requested GPU device IDs <ids>: <exc>', and exit code 1. It fails closed: no partial or empty result set is returned as success, the requested GPU ids and the exception text reach stderr, and the exit code is 1. It does not fall back to a different engine, which would break the explicit-GPU contract.

The failure is not hidden. A parent that only checks the process return code and not response.exit_code would miss it, but that is the protocol contract, and the traceback is kept in full.

The restore loops use narrow except OSError: pass clauses, so a failed rollback write is not disclosed. That residual is a separate narrow handler outside this record, and the primary failure is still raised.

It is not a trust decision: the string is informational provenance, the receipt is still signed and verified over whatever value was written, and no gate keys off it. evidence: except Exception around repo_map.build_symbol_blast_radius(query, path) on the opt-in --recompute path: on any failure the blast_radius block becomes {status: 'unavailable', reason: 'recompute failed: <exc>'}; the receipt is still built. The result is not stale or partial: a full rebuild is what the non-incremental path would have produced, and the snapshot and generation are captured after it, so the refreshed session cannot pass off an unrefreshed map as fresh. evidence: except Exception around the per-request body of the stream serve loop (including serve_session_request and the refresh_on_stale recovery path): the request gets an error response {version, session_id, error: {code: 'invalid_request', message: str(exc)}} written to the response stream and flushed, and the loop continues with the next line. The failure is not logged server-side, so an operator relies on the client seeing the error code. evidence: except Exception around the 'ping' _daemon_request to the daemon recorded in daemon.json (connect refused, timeout, bad response, unauthorized): the probe returns None, the module's defined 'no live daemon' value.
